topics.title: § 4.3.1 — Findings, Reasons & Reviewability (pp. 190–198)
topics.description: Classes 13–14 · APA § 557(c), MSAPA § 12, Ship Creek, T-Mobile, detailed subsidiary findings and Type C denials.

entries.title: Why agency findings and reasons are required
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 190–191
entries.summary: Formal federal APA § 557(c) requires findings, conclusions and grounds on material issues of fact, law and discretion; 1961 MSAPA § 12 requires written findings and conclusions with supporting underlying facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Formal federal APA § 557(c) requires findings, conclusions and grounds on material issues of fact, law and discretion; 1961 MSAPA § 12 requires written findings and conclusions with supporting underlying facts.
entries.legalExplanation: The decision cannot be a mysterious yes/no; it should explain what was found and how it supports the result.
entries.examApplication: Reasons permit meaningful judicial review, improve decision quality, clarify party options and guard against agencies exceeding authority.
entries.examTrap: Separate findings of fact from conclusions of law and policy-discretion explanations.

entries.title: Ship Creek Hydraulic Syndicate v. State, 685 P.2d 715 (Alaska 1984)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 191–194
entries.summary: Yes, prospectively. Agencies making important individualized quick-take decisions should provide a contemporaneous reasoned document identifying decisive considerations; rule was not applied retroactively against this state taking.
entries.laymanExplanation: Yes, prospectively. Agencies making important individualized quick-take decisions should provide a contemporaneous reasoned document identifying decisive considerations; rule was not applied retroactively against this state taking.
entries.legalExplanation: Could Alaska require a contemporaneous decisional document explaining reasons for land condemnation to support statutory judicial review? A clear document improves deliberation, permits owners to decide whether to challenge and facilitates review of statutory factors. Court distinguished Vermont Yankee because review records can be organized without imposing incompatible federal-style procedural rules.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Alaska used quick-take highway condemnation procedure despite statutory requirement to choose routing compatible with greatest public good and least private injury. State used formulaic one-sentence declaration rather than contemporaneous explanation of the individualized location decision.
entries.issue: Could Alaska require a contemporaneous decisional document explaining reasons for land condemnation to support statutory judicial review?
entries.holding: Yes, prospectively. Agencies making important individualized quick-take decisions should provide a contemporaneous reasoned document identifying decisive considerations; rule was not applied retroactively against this state taking.
entries.reasoning: A clear document improves deliberation, permits owners to decide whether to challenge and facilitates review of statutory factors. Court distinguished Vermont Yankee because review records can be organized without imposing incompatible federal-style procedural rules.
entries.rule: Where statute obliges individualized comparative factors in condemnation, agency should state principal facts and determinative reasons contemporaneously in a reviewable document.
entries.examApplication: Explain source of reason-giving (state statutory review/inherent courts' review needs) and prospective nature of remedy; distinguish generalized conclusory assertions from actual findings.
entries.examTrap: Court affirmed the particular taking because applying new duty retroactively would impose unfair burden.

entries.title: Contemporaneous decisional documents
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 192–194
entries.summary: Decision should identify determinative reasons, essential facts and seriously disputed issues, without requiring lengthy formulaic opinion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Decision should identify determinative reasons, essential facts and seriously disputed issues, without requiring lengthy formulaic opinion.
entries.legalExplanation: A brief clear explanation is better than repeating a statute.
entries.examApplication: Ship Creek treated reason-giving as instrumental to judicial review and intrinsically respectful of affected owners; court left form flexible.
entries.examTrap: Check whether reasons were made when agency acted or manufactured after litigation began.

entries.title: SEACC v. State, 665 P.2d 544 (Alaska 1983)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 192, 194–195
entries.summary: In timber-contract setting, urged reasons identifying material premises and supporting review.
entries.laymanExplanation: In timber-contract setting, urged reasons identifying material premises and supporting review.
entries.legalExplanation: Ship Creek drew on earlier discretionary decision and recognized good decisional record.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Identify statutory and judicial-review connection.

entries.title: Vermont Yankee limit versus need for reviewable record
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 193–195
entries.summary: Federal reviewing courts cannot invent additional adjudicatory procedural requirements beyond law, but may remand for explanation necessary to review agency action.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal reviewing courts cannot invent additional adjudicatory procedural requirements beyond law, but may remand for explanation necessary to review agency action.
entries.legalExplanation: Judges cannot prescribe new agency trial procedures just because preferred, yet can require agency to explain why it acted.
entries.examApplication: Text contrasts Ship Creek state-law requirement with Vermont Yankee and PBGC federal constraints and review of unexplained actions.
entries.examTrap: Identify actual source of obligation: APA, specific statute, due process, or reviewing court's need to assess compliance.

entries.title: T-Mobile South, LLC v. City of Roswell, 574 U.S. 293 (2015)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 195–196
entries.summary: Telecommunications Act's 'in writing and supported by substantial evidence in written record' demands clear reasons for denied wireless-tower permit.
entries.laymanExplanation: Telecommunications Act's 'in writing and supported by substantial evidence in written record' demands clear reasons for denied wireless-tower permit.
entries.legalExplanation: Written reasons may appear in contemporaneously available minutes rather than denial letter if communicated essentially with denial.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Explain no substantial-evidence review can occur without knowing what municipality decided and why.

entries.title: Subsidiary findings link evidence to legal conclusion
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 196
entries.summary: Agency cannot merely rehearse contradictory testimony or repeat statutory words; must decide which relevant facts actually occurred and how they establish legal standards.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency cannot merely rehearse contradictory testimony or repeat statutory words; must decide which relevant facts actually occurred and how they establish legal standards.
entries.legalExplanation: The decision must say what happened, not just list what witnesses said.
entries.examApplication: 1961 MSAPA § 12 demands underlying facts if using legal conclusions; Adams worker-compensation decision lacked meaningful findings on disputed causation.
entries.examTrap: Illustrate missing factual bridge: medical experts disagree but ruling only says 'not work related'.

entries.title: Adams v. Board of Review, 821 P.2d 1 (Utah Ct. App. 1991)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 196
entries.summary: Workers' compensation ruling had no subsidiary findings on contested medical causation and was reversed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Workers' compensation ruling had no subsidiary findings on contested medical causation and was reversed.
entries.legalExplanation: Summary of testimony plus ultimate conclusion is insufficient to demonstrate decision path.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Define subsidiary finding, not just ultimate issue.

entries.title: Adopting an ALJ decision and intermediate reasons
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 196–197
entries.summary: Agency appellate head may adopt sufficient initial decision without repeating reasoning; but vague selective affirmation may leave uncertainty about which findings stand.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency appellate head may adopt sufficient initial decision without repeating reasoning; but vague selective affirmation may leave uncertainty about which findings stand.
entries.legalExplanation: One well-explained decision can suffice; if the boss changes findings, they must make clear which.
entries.examApplication: Guentchev approves adoption of earlier opinion; Armstrong rejects opaque affirmation of only 'substantially correct' result.
entries.examTrap: Check record clarity and whether changed portions are explained.

entries.title: Guentchev v. INS, 77 F.3d 1036 (7th Cir. 1996)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 196–197
entries.summary: Board can adopt a prior reasoned opinion without restating its reasoning.
entries.laymanExplanation: Board can adopt a prior reasoned opinion without restating its reasoning.
entries.legalExplanation: No requirement to reword adequately supported initial decision.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast with Armstrong.

entries.title: Armstrong v. CFTC, 12 F.3d 401 (3d Cir. 1993)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 197
entries.summary: Agency's vague approval of a 'substantially correct' ALJ result left unresolved what findings it rejected.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency's vague approval of a 'substantially correct' ALJ result left unresolved what findings it rejected.
entries.legalExplanation: Insufficient under APA § 557(c).
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Clarify difference from full adoption.

entries.title: Reason-giving in Type C under APA § 555(e)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 197–198
entries.summary: When agency denies a written application, petition or other request by interested person, it ordinarily must give prompt notice and brief grounds, except self-explanatory denial or affirming prior denial.
entries.laymanExplanation: When agency denies a written application, petition or other request by interested person, it ordinarily must give prompt notice and brief grounds, except self-explanatory denial or affirming prior denial.
entries.legalExplanation: Even informal agency decisions denying requests should normally say why.
entries.examApplication: Tourus Records found 'not adequately supported' indigency waiver denial too conclusory; ACUS Recommendation 2023-5 urges broader plain-language reasons proportionate to stakes, but is nonbinding.
entries.examTrap: For Type C government benefits, grant, waiver, FOIA or licensing-type request, assess whether denial gives real explanation.

entries.title: Tourus Records, Inc. v. DEA, 259 F.3d 731 (D.C. Cir. 2001)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 197–198
entries.summary: DEA's bare refusal to waive forfeiture bond without reasons violated APA § 555(e).
entries.laymanExplanation: DEA's bare refusal to waive forfeiture bond without reasons violated APA § 555(e).
entries.legalExplanation: A conclusion is not a statement of reasoning; parties need to know defect and courts need reviewable grounds.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Examine what additional facts/grounds agency should provide.

topics.title: § 4.3.2 — Post Hoc Rationalization & Remand (pp. 198–203)
topics.description: Classes 13–14 · Calcutt, Chenery I, post hoc lawyer justifications, DACA Regents, updated genuine decisions.

entries.title: Chenery I: review on grounds actually relied on
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 198–201
entries.summary: A reviewing court judges agency action on the grounds agency invoked; it cannot itself create a better rationale after finding explanation legally defective.
entries.laymanExplanation: A reviewing court judges agency action on the grounds agency invoked; it cannot itself create a better rationale after finding explanation legally defective.
entries.legalExplanation: Even if government could win on another ground, the court cannot invent the agency's reasoning.
entries.examApplication: Absent narrow inevitable-result exception, courts remand legal or factual deficiencies to accountable agency decisionmakers, not counsel or appellate judges.
entries.examTrap: Identify original reason, precise legal error and whether remand discretion exists.

entries.title: Calcutt v. FDIC, 598 U.S. 623 (2023)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 198–200
entries.summary: No. Except narrow inevitability, ordinary remand rule required returning discretionary sanctions to FDIC for correct legal and factual evaluation.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Except narrow inevitability, ordinary remand rule required returning discretionary sanctions to FDIC for correct legal and factual evaluation.
entries.legalExplanation: Can reviewing court preserve discretionary agency sanctions after finding legal flaws in the actual FDIC decision by substituting its own causal and remedial assessment? Bank harm, proximate cause and sanction severity were contextual and discretionary; appellate panel exceeded its role by reasoning FDIC would probably impose same sanctions.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: FDIC sanctioned bank CEO Calcutt for unsafe lending losses, imposed $125,000 penalty and industry bar. Sixth Circuit found board misapplied statutory causation and injury, yet affirmed under its own narrower rationale.
entries.issue: Can reviewing court preserve discretionary agency sanctions after finding legal flaws in the actual FDIC decision by substituting its own causal and remedial assessment?
entries.holding: No. Except narrow inevitability, ordinary remand rule required returning discretionary sanctions to FDIC for correct legal and factual evaluation.
entries.reasoning: Bank harm, proximate cause and sanction severity were contextual and discretionary; appellate panel exceeded its role by reasoning FDIC would probably impose same sanctions.
entries.rule: If agency's grounds fail, court ordinarily remands to agency; only where outcome is legally mandatory and certain may explanation defect be harmless.
entries.examApplication: Highlight discretionary sanctions and fact-specific causation; distinguish rare legally foreordained agency action.
entries.examTrap: The Sixth Circuit's substituted analysis was reversed, not merely criticized as suboptimal.

entries.title: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), 318 U.S. 80 (1943)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 199–201
entries.summary: Court may not uphold agency action by supplying substitute grounds absent agency adoption.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court may not uphold agency action by supplying substitute grounds absent agency adoption.
entries.legalExplanation: Foundational review-on-actual-grounds principle.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply to attorneys' litigation briefs and Calcutt.

entries.title: Florida Power & Light Corp. v. Lorion, 470 U.S. 729 (1985)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 199–201
entries.summary: Inadequate grounds or missing inquiry generally require remand to agency.
entries.laymanExplanation: Inadequate grounds or missing inquiry generally require remand to agency.
entries.legalExplanation: Ordinary remand allows proper investigation/explanation from authorized actor.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Cite with Calcutt and Chenery.

entries.title: Narrow inevitability exception
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 199–201
entries.summary: Remand may be unnecessary only if the agency was legally required to take exact action and no uncertainty exists about outcome.
entries.laymanExplanation: Remand may be unnecessary only if the agency was legally required to take exact action and no uncertainty exists about outcome.
entries.legalExplanation: A court avoids remand only where agency has zero legal choice left.
entries.examApplication: Calcutt refused shortcut because bank sanctions were discretionary in type and severity.
entries.examTrap: Check whether statute mandates result after corrected legal test.

entries.title: Agency litigation explanations after the decision
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 200–201
entries.summary: Lawyers cannot supply decisive novel agency justifications at appellate stage that heads did not adopt contemporaneously.
entries.laymanExplanation: Lawyers cannot supply decisive novel agency justifications at appellate stage that heads did not adopt contemporaneously.
entries.legalExplanation: Government cannot change its story in a court brief to rescue earlier unexplained action.
entries.examApplication: Chenery I emphasizes agency accountability and reviewability; Overton Park permitted limited record inquiry but later cases favor agency remand for explanation.
entries.examTrap: Separate permissible elaboration of actual old grounds from new after-the-fact reason.

entries.title: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe, 401 U.S. 402 (1971)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 200–201
entries.summary: Original park-road funding decision lacked explanation for no feasible prudent alternative.
entries.laymanExplanation: Original park-road funding decision lacked explanation for no feasible prudent alternative.
entries.legalExplanation: Book discusses shift toward remand to agency rather than district court reconstruction.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Compare reviewing record with post hoc substitute reasoning.

entries.title: DACA rescission — old explanation versus new agency decision
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 201–203
entries.summary: Regents rejected DHS Secretary Nielsen's later memo as post hoc explanation of Duke's earlier 2017 DACA rescission, not a genuine new independent decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: Regents rejected DHS Secretary Nielsen's later memo as post hoc explanation of Duke's earlier 2017 DACA rescission, not a genuine new independent decision.
entries.legalExplanation: An agency can make a fresh decision, but cannot retroactively paste new policy arguments onto an old one.
entries.examApplication: The Court distinguished simultaneous contemporaneous explanation from 2018 reasons for already completed action; new reasoning requires actual new agency action, not belated memo saying prior order stands.
entries.examTrap: Identify precise agency action under review and whether later memo rescinds/replaces it.

entries.title: DHS v. Regents of the University of California (2020)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 201–203
entries.summary: Later DHS policy justifications did not cure the earlier DACA rescission; rescission held arbitrary and capricious.
entries.laymanExplanation: Later DHS policy justifications did not cure the earlier DACA rescission; rescission held arbitrary and capricious.
entries.legalExplanation: Nielsen declined to disturb Duke order and supplied explanations rather than redoing decision; Court protected public response and stable review targets.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast new decision in Biden v. Texas.

entries.title: Biden v. Texas, 597 U.S. 785 (2022)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 202–203
entries.summary: Later agency termination of Remain in Mexico policy reviewed on new reasons where old decision no longer existed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Later agency termination of Remain in Mexico policy reviewed on new reasons where old decision no longer existed.
entries.legalExplanation: Genuine new decision is not post hoc repair of prior existing order.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Identify replacement versus supplementation.

topics.title: § 4.4.2 — Agency Precedents & Stare Decisis (pp. 210–212)
topics.description: Classes 13–14 · UAW, changes in policy through adjudication, explaining deviations from prior law.

entries.title: Administrative agency may change its policy with an explanation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 210–212
entries.summary: Agencies are not strictly bound by stare decisis like courts, but cannot silently depart from well-established positions; must identify and reasonably justify changes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies are not strictly bound by stare decisis like courts, but cannot silently depart from well-established positions; must identify and reasonably justify changes.
entries.legalExplanation: An agency can change its mind, but must admit that it changed course and explain why.
entries.examApplication: Agencies may make policy through adjudication or rulemaking; consistency, legal reliance, transparency and meaningful review demand explanation for policy shifts.
entries.examTrap: Compare existing agency decisions with new decision and ask whether agency acknowledged departure.

entries.title: United Automobile Workers v. NLRB, 802 F.2d 969 (7th Cir. 1986)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 210–211
entries.summary: No. Agency may revise statutory interpretation but must acknowledge change and give reasoned justification; decision set aside and remanded.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Agency may revise statutory interpretation but must acknowledge change and give reasoned justification; decision set aside and remanded.
entries.legalExplanation: May NLRB effectively alter well-established presumption against waiver without discussing departure from existing agency policy? Board's refusal to mention controlling agency doctrine was not sufficient, even if it intended a policy change. Common-law adjudication does not exempt agencies from duty to explain about-faces.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Employer agreed to 'discuss' plant relocation with union; NLRB treated wording as union waiver of right to 'negotiate' labor-cost-motivated relocation, without addressing earlier clear-and-unmistakable waiver precedent invoked by union.
entries.issue: May NLRB effectively alter well-established presumption against waiver without discussing departure from existing agency policy?
entries.holding: No. Agency may revise statutory interpretation but must acknowledge change and give reasoned justification; decision set aside and remanded.
entries.reasoning: Board's refusal to mention controlling agency doctrine was not sufficient, even if it intended a policy change. Common-law adjudication does not exempt agencies from duty to explain about-faces.
entries.rule: Agency may abandon precedent only after adequately explicating basis of new interpretation; unexplained policy shifts are invalid in adjudication as in rulemaking.
entries.examApplication: Identify prior waiver presumption, new interpretation of 'discuss,' and absence of explanation; contrast permissibility of new rule with reason-giving duty.
entries.examTrap: Do not say NLRB is permanently bound by its old waiver policy.

entries.title: Rulemaking versus adjudication to make policy
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 210–212
entries.summary: Agency may formulate or change regulatory policy by deciding cases instead of adopting general rules, but adjudicatory route still needs explanations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency may formulate or change regulatory policy by deciding cases instead of adopting general rules, but adjudicatory route still needs explanations.
entries.legalExplanation: An agency can build policy one case at a time, but policy shifts cannot be disguised as unchanged rules.
entries.examApplication: UAW invokes Bell Aerospace as agency option to choose procedures while imposing explanation obligation on substantive changes.
entries.examTrap: Discuss retroactivity and fairness when case-based new standard applies to parties already acting.

entries.title: NLRB v. Bell Aerospace Co. (discussed in § 6.2)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 210–211
entries.summary: Agency has substantial choice between adjudication and rulemaking for new policy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency has substantial choice between adjudication and rulemaking for new policy.
entries.legalExplanation: UAW cited it to reject loophole evading reason-giving via individual cases.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Identify whether change occurred via order rather than rule.

entries.title: Flagstaff Broadcasting Foundation v. FCC, 979 F.2d 1566 (D.C. Cir. 1992)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 212
entries.summary: Court required adequate response to serious argument against existing broadcast-licensing policy, not bare reliance on precedent.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court required adequate response to serious argument against existing broadcast-licensing policy, not bare reliance on precedent.
entries.legalExplanation: Illustrates duty to give reasons even when agency says it is staying the course.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast explanation for abandoning policy versus reflexive refusal to reconsider.

topics.title: § 4.5.1 — Fair Notice of Legal Standards (pp. 212–219)
topics.description: Classes 13–14 · Fox II, regulatory vagueness, retrospective enforcement, reliance, p. 218 professor-assigned problem.

entries.title: Fair notice of what conduct the regulation forbids
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 212–215
entries.summary: Administrative sanctions must respect due process: ordinary person must have fair notice of prohibited or required behavior; standards cannot be so vague they invite arbitrary enforcement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Administrative sanctions must respect due process: ordinary person must have fair notice of prohibited or required behavior; standards cannot be so vague they invite arbitrary enforcement.
entries.legalExplanation: Government cannot punish you under a surprise rule nobody could reasonably discern beforehand.
entries.examApplication: Different from notice of hearing charges. Legality of agency policy changes under APA is distinct from retroactive sanctions without fair warning.
entries.examTrap: Identify regulation's text, prior official interpretations and how sudden changed enforcement affects regulated conduct.

entries.title: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (Fox II), 567 U.S. 239 (2012)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 213–217
entries.summary: No. Abrupt application of changed indecency standards to earlier Fox and ABC broadcasts violated due process fair notice; orders set aside without deciding policy's present First Amendment validity.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Abrupt application of changed indecency standards to earlier Fox and ABC broadcasts violated due process fair notice; orders set aside without deciding policy's present First Amendment validity.
entries.legalExplanation: Did FCC give constitutionally adequate fair notice before treating pre-change fleeting incidents as actionable indecency? Earlier policy led broadcasters to think isolated incidents were not actionable. FCC later treated them as violations. Fox's record of violation could have future legal effects even without present fine; ABC faced substantial fine. Media speech raises heightened sensitivity to vagueness.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: FCC previously distinguished repeated broadcast indecency from isolated fleeting expletives/nudity. Fox aired unscripted fleeting expletives in 2002–2003; ABC aired brief nudity in 2003. FCC later adopted a stricter Golden Globes enforcement policy and applied it to these earlier broadcasts.
entries.issue: Did FCC give constitutionally adequate fair notice before treating pre-change fleeting incidents as actionable indecency?
entries.holding: No. Abrupt application of changed indecency standards to earlier Fox and ABC broadcasts violated due process fair notice; orders set aside without deciding policy's present First Amendment validity.
entries.reasoning: Earlier policy led broadcasters to think isolated incidents were not actionable. FCC later treated them as violations. Fox's record of violation could have future legal effects even without present fine; ABC faced substantial fine. Media speech raises heightened sensitivity to vagueness.
entries.rule: Agencies may prospectively revise interpretations but cannot impose penalties for past conduct without fair notice under governing standard at the time.
entries.examApplication: Separately analyze fair notice, vagueness, reputational/status effects, actual penalties, and distinction between Fox I APA policy-change justification and Fox II due process.
entries.examTrap: Court deliberately did not invalidate FCC's entire current policy or decide broad First Amendment merits.

entries.title: Fox I versus Fox II
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 213–217
entries.summary: Fox I (2009) addressed APA arbitrary-and-capricious standards for agency policy change; Fox II (2012) addressed due process notice as applied to particular earlier broadcasts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Fox I (2009) addressed APA arbitrary-and-capricious standards for agency policy change; Fox II (2012) addressed due process notice as applied to particular earlier broadcasts.
entries.legalExplanation: Changing a policy can be rational as a regulatory matter and still unfair to punish pre-change behavior.
entries.examApplication: Fox I generally requires acknowledgement and reason for changed position, not necessarily showing new policy better; Fox II prohibits unanticipated retrospective sanctions.
entries.examTrap: Present the constitutional and APA grounds separately.

entries.title: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (Fox I), 556 U.S. 502 (2009)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 214–215
entries.summary: Policy change need not be justified as inherently better than old policy, but must be acknowledged with good reasons.
entries.laymanExplanation: Policy change need not be justified as inherently better than old policy, but must be acknowledged with good reasons.
entries.legalExplanation: Earlier phase of same litigation concerned APA change-of-course review rather than fair notice of prior broadcasts.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast Fox II retroactivity.

entries.title: Reputation and future legal consequences can matter
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 215–216
entries.summary: Even absent current fine, official wrongdoing finding may raise later sanctions or reputational harm that prevents treating notice error as harmless.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even absent current fine, official wrongdoing finding may raise later sanctions or reputational harm that prevents treating notice error as harmless.
entries.legalExplanation: A warning on record can injure even if government promises not to use it right now.
entries.examApplication: Fox II noted FCC legal authority to count past violations when calculating penalties, plus reputation with viewers and advertisers.
entries.examTrap: Examine real legal/market consequences when agency says no sanction was imposed.

entries.title: General Electric Co. v. EPA, 53 F.3d 1324 (D.C. Cir. 1995)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 217
entries.summary: EPA could not fine regulated party for adopting a reasonable interpretation of ambiguous PCB regulation without advance notice of agency's different position.
entries.laymanExplanation: EPA could not fine regulated party for adopting a reasonable interpretation of ambiguous PCB regulation without advance notice of agency's different position.
entries.legalExplanation: Book treats it as pre-Fox II use of administrative fair-warning doctrine.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Apply outside First Amendment setting when regulation is ambiguous.

entries.title: Retroactive adjudicatory change as manifest injustice
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 217–218
entries.summary: A new adjudicatory interpretation generally applies retroactively, but court may find manifest injustice if reliance and surprise outweigh statutory enforcement goals.
entries.laymanExplanation: A new adjudicatory interpretation generally applies retroactively, but court may find manifest injustice if reliance and surprise outweigh statutory enforcement goals.
entries.legalExplanation: Agencies commonly develop new law while deciding old cases, but some retroactive penalties are too unfair.
entries.examApplication: Retail, Wholesale & Department Store Union balances first-impression status, abrupt departure, extent of reliance, burden of order and statutory enforcement interest; later cases simplify to equity/fairness.
entries.examTrap: Use five factors, then evaluate reasonableness of reliance and seriousness of retroactive harm.

entries.title: Retail, Wholesale & Department Store Union v. NLRB, 466 F.2d 380 (D.C. Cir. 1972)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 217–218

entries.laymanExplanation: New NLRB rehire interpretation applied retrospectively to Coca-Cola produced manifest injustice, invalidating reinstatement/back-pay order.
entries.legalExplanation: Five-factor balancing test protects settled reliance against harsh retroactive agency adjudication.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: List and apply factors.

topics.title: § 4.5.2 — Equitable Estoppel, Agency Advice & Declaratory Orders (pp. 219–224)
topics.description: Classes 13–14 · OPM v. Richmond, statutory government payments, misleading advice, state/federal approaches, p. 223 professor problem.

entries.title: Equitable estoppel elements and special government limits
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 219–223
entries.summary: Ordinarily a party making misleading statement cannot contradict it after another reasonably and detrimentally relies; against government, serious separation-of-powers and appropriation limits restrict estoppel.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ordinarily a party making misleading statement cannot contradict it after another reasonably and detrimentally relies; against government, serious separation-of-powers and appropriation limits restrict estoppel.
entries.legalExplanation: Incorrect government advice does not always create a legal entitlement.
entries.examApplication: Evaluate actual misrepresentation, authority, reasonable reliance, detrimental change and legality of promised relief. Federal appropriated money cannot be paid contrary to statute.
entries.examTrap: Distinguish federal Treasury payment from possible state-law estoppel for tax collection or procedural filing.

entries.title: Office of Personnel Management v. Richmond, 496 U.S. 414 (1990)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 219–221
entries.summary: No. Appropriations Clause prohibits payment from federal Treasury inconsistent with congressional appropriation; Court did not decide whether any government estoppel claim could succeed in another setting.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Appropriations Clause prohibits payment from federal Treasury inconsistent with congressional appropriation; Court did not decide whether any government estoppel claim could succeed in another setting.
entries.legalExplanation: Could mistaken advice by federal official estop government from denying payments unambiguously unauthorized by governing statute? Enforcing promised unlawful benefit would let officials override Congress and create public-fisc uncertainty; broad estoppel might discourage agencies from furnishing helpful public guidance.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion reproduced in supplied chapter
entries.facts: Retired Navy employee Richmond was told incorrectly by government personnel officer that taking extra work would not interrupt disability retirement payments, did so, and lost benefits for six months.
entries.issue: Could mistaken advice by federal official estop government from denying payments unambiguously unauthorized by governing statute?
entries.holding: No. Appropriations Clause prohibits payment from federal Treasury inconsistent with congressional appropriation; Court did not decide whether any government estoppel claim could succeed in another setting.
entries.reasoning: Enforcing promised unlawful benefit would let officials override Congress and create public-fisc uncertainty; broad estoppel might discourage agencies from furnishing helpful public guidance.
entries.rule: Estoppel cannot compel federal payments contrary to statutory appropriation, even after reliance on erroneous official advice.
entries.examApplication: Identify whether asserted remedy demands unlawful government payment, and if not, distinguish reserved broader issue.
entries.examTrap: The Court rejected Treasury-money claim, not every conceivable government estoppel case.

entries.title: Appropriations Clause barrier
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 219–221
entries.summary: Article I, § 9, cl. 7 places expenditure authority in Congress; executive misunderstandings do not authorize benefits inconsistent with statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Article I, § 9, cl. 7 places expenditure authority in Congress; executive misunderstandings do not authorize benefits inconsistent with statute.
entries.legalExplanation: Government staff cannot promise money Congress did not legally appropriate.
entries.examApplication: Richmond relies on institutional controls over public funds and avoiding unofficial rewrites of statutory benefit schemes.
entries.examTrap: Ask whether monetary remedy would require law-defying disbursement.

entries.title: State estoppel can protect innocent reliance
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 221–222
entries.summary: Some states apply equitable estoppel against their governments when official mistake caused reasonable harm without subverting the regulatory statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some states apply equitable estoppel against their governments when official mistake caused reasonable harm without subverting the regulatory statute.
entries.legalExplanation: A state may sometimes waive collection after a trusted agent gave wrong filing advice.
entries.examApplication: Foote's Dixie Dandy estopped Arkansas from collecting extra unemployment tax when routine corporate form could have been timely filed but staff incorrectly said none was needed.
entries.examTrap: Check state-specific doctrine, limited remedial scope and good-faith reliance.

entries.title: Foote's Dixie Dandy, Inc. v. McHenry, 607 S.W.2d 323 (Ark. 1980)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 221–222
entries.summary: State estopped from collecting additional unemployment tax due to erroneous field-agent advice and innocent reliance.
entries.laymanExplanation: State estopped from collecting additional unemployment tax due to erroneous field-agent advice and innocent reliance.
entries.legalExplanation: Filing would have been routinely approved, and no bad faith undermined fairness.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Contrast Richmond's forbidden federal Treasury outlay.

entries.title: Heckler v. Community Health Services, 467 U.S. 51 (1984)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 222–223
entries.summary: Government estoppel not established where clinic relied on oral intermediary advice and merely had to repay improperly received Medicare money.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government estoppel not established where clinic relied on oral intermediary advice and merely had to repay improperly received Medicare money.
entries.legalExplanation: Court assumed arguendo possible estoppel but found neither sufficiently reasonable nor detrimental reliance.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not reproduced
entries.examApplication: Check oral statement, source, written confirmation and genuine detrimental position change.

entries.title: Limits of oral advice and actual detrimental reliance
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 222–223
entries.summary: Reliance on uncertain verbal guidance from intermediaries is less reasonable; repaying wrongly received payments does not alone mean relinquishing a protected legal right.
entries.laymanExplanation: Reliance on uncertain verbal guidance from intermediaries is less reasonable; repaying wrongly received payments does not alone mean relinquishing a protected legal right.
entries.legalExplanation: Not every budget disappointment counts as legal detriment.
entries.examApplication: Heckler v. Community Health Services focused on reasonable reliance and change of position, rather than adopting absolute bar.
entries.examTrap: Investigate who spoke, their authority, form of guidance, and specific losses from relying.

entries.title: Declaratory orders as safer advance binding advice
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 223
entries.summary: APA § 554(e) authorizes declaratory orders that bind agency and parties on stipulated facts, unlike informal advice letters; judicial review may follow.
entries.laymanExplanation: APA § 554(e) authorizes declaratory orders that bind agency and parties on stipulated facts, unlike informal advice letters; judicial review may follow.
entries.legalExplanation: Instead of informal employee assurances, request a binding official declaration of what law means for known facts.
entries.examApplication: Book notes uncertainty whether declaratory-order authority is available in Types B/C where federal formal gateway does not open; court can review actual order.
entries.examTrap: Recommend considering binding agency order as distinct from suing on a mistaken advice letter.

entries.title: Policy tradeoff: advice availability versus individual hardship
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), ch. 4, pp. 220–223
entries.summary: Richmond worried automatic estoppel would deter government advice and create unpredictable public expense; state cases and textbook critique emphasize fairness to people who cannot know every regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Richmond worried automatic estoppel would deter government advice and create unpredictable public expense; state cases and textbook critique emphasize fairness to people who cannot know every regulation.
entries.legalExplanation: Should government fear liability for bad advice, or should individuals be able to trust public officials?
entries.examApplication: Frame competing arguments without misrepresenting Richmond's narrow holding, and distinguish formal declaratory order from gratuitous guidance.
entries.examTrap: Use policy debate in essay without inventing extra legal test.
